deck.title: IAM — Identity and Access Management
deck.analogy: AWS is a giant office building: IAM hands out badges (users), departments (groups), temporary costumes (roles), and policies are the rules on the wall saying which badges open which doors.

subtopics.title: How AWS decides yes or no
STS and roles: how the costume gets put on
IAM Identity Center (the artist formerly known as AWS SSO)

cards.front: What two questions does IAM answer, and what is its scope and cost?

back.answer: Who are you? and Are you allowed to do that? IAM is free and global (not region-bound).
back.explanation: IAM is the front door, ID checker and rulebook in one.
back.mnemonic: AWS is an office building; IAM hands out badges.

cards.front: In the IAM office-building analogy, what are users, groups, roles and policies?

back.answer: User = permanent badge; group = department; role = temporary costume; policy = rules on the wall.
back.explanation: The temporary-costume role idea is the most exam-tested IAM concept.

cards.front: IAM user: what is it and when do you use it?

back.answer: Permanent identity for one human (or legacy app) with password and/or long-lived access keys.
back.explanation: Use for a specific person who needs AWS access.

cards.front: IAM group: what can it contain?

back.answer: Only users — never other groups, never roles. Used to manage permissions by team.

cards.front: IAM role: what credentials does it have and when is it used?

back.answer: No password or permanent keys; it is assumed and hands out temporary credentials. For services, cross-account, federated humans.
back.mnemonic: A temporary costume anyone can put on.

cards.front: How should EC2, Lambda and ECS tasks get AWS permissions?

back.answer: EC2: instance role (instance profile). Lambda: execution role. ECS: task role.
back.explanation: EC2 fetches auto-rotating temporary credentials from metadata; no keys touch the disk.

cards.front: IAM trap: an answer says to store access keys on the instance, in the AMI, env variables or code. Correct?

back.answer: Wrong. The right answer is always the IAM role.
back.explanation: Hardcoded credentials on EC2: fix by attaching an IAM role to the instance. Keys leak and never self-rotate.

cards.front: IAM policy: what are the Effect values?

back.answer: Only Allow or Deny.

cards.front: IAM policy: what do Action, Resource and Condition specify?

back.answer: Action = API calls (service prefix + verb); Resource = ARN of things; Condition = optional "only if" clauses.
back.explanation: ARN is AWS's globally unique ID string. Conditions can require MFA, an IP range, or HTTPS.

cards.front: Why do IAM resource-based policies have a Principal field?

back.answer: They attach to a resource, not an identity, so they must name who the statement applies to.

cards.front: IAM policy evaluation: what are the three core rules?

back.answer: Default implicit deny; an Allow opens the door; an explicit Deny always wins.
back.explanation: Explicit Deny beats any Allow, anywhere, no exceptions.

cards.sourceHeading: How AWS decides yes or no

cards.front: IAM: what gates must a request pass to succeed?

back.answer: SCP, resource policy, permission boundary and identity policy must allow; any explicit Deny blocks it.
back.explanation: An SCP or explicit Deny blocks everything downstream.

cards.sourceHeading: How AWS decides yes or no

cards.front: IAM trap: a user's policy says Allow but the action fails. Why?

back.answer: An explicit Deny, an SCP on the account, or a permission boundary. Allow + Deny = Deny.
back.explanation: SCP is common when the question mentions AWS Organizations.

cards.sourceHeading: How AWS decides yes or no

cards.front: IAM identity-based policy: attached to what and what does it do?

back.answer: Attached to a user, group or role; the everyday "what can this identity do".

cards.front: IAM resource-based policy: attached to what and what does it enable?

back.answer: Attached to the resource (e.g. S3 bucket or SQS queue policy); has a Principal; enables cross-account grants.
back.explanation: "Who can touch me."

cards.front: IAM permission boundary: what does it do?

back.answer: A maximum ceiling for one user or role; grants nothing. Effective = identity policy ∩ boundary.

cards.front: AWS Organizations SCP: what does it do and does it affect root?

back.answer: Org-wide ceiling on accounts/OUs; grants nothing; caps everyone in the account including its root user.
back.mnemonic: SCP = ceiling for a whole account.

cards.front: IAM session policy: when is it used and what does it do?

back.answer: Passed when assuming a role; shrinks that one session's permissions further.

cards.front: S3 ACL: what is it and how does it differ from a Network ACL?

back.answer: Legacy S3-only grant mechanism; no JSON conditions; use bucket policies. Network ACL is an unrelated VPC subnet firewall.
back.explanation: S3 ACLs cannot grant to users in their own account.

cards.front: Permission boundary vs SCP: scope and whether either grants permissions?

back.answer: Boundary caps one identity; SCP caps a whole account; neither grants anything.

cards.front: Developers may create IAM roles but never ones more powerful than X. Which feature?

back.answer: Permission boundary, required on every role they create.

cards.front: What does STS return on sts:AssumeRole, and how long is it valid?

back.answer: Temporary credentials (access key, secret key, session token), 15 min to 12 h, default 1 hour.
back.explanation: They expire on their own; nothing to rotate or leak long-term.
back.mnemonic: STS = coat-check counter handing out costumes.

cards.sourceHeading: STS and roles: how the costume gets put on

cards.front: IAM role permissions policy vs trust policy?

back.answer: Permissions policy = what the role can do; trust policy = who may assume it.
back.explanation: The trust policy is a resource-based policy on the role naming the trusted principal.

cards.sourceHeading: STS and roles: how the costume gets put on

cards.front: IAM role has the right permissions but a user/service can't assume it. What to check?

back.answer: The trust policy.
back.explanation: Permissions say what the role can do; trust says who can wear it.

cards.sourceHeading: STS and roles: how the costume gets put on

cards.front: IAM cross-account: what are the steps for Account A to access Account B's S3 bucket?

back.answer: B creates a role with permissions and trusts A; A's users get sts:AssumeRole on the role ARN, assume it, get temporary credentials.
back.explanation: No shared passwords or duplicated users.

choices.text: Share an access key from Account B
Duplicate IAM users in Account A
choices.why: Duplicated users are not the recipe.

choices.text: Role in B trusting A; A users AssumeRole

cards.front: IAM trust policy: what is ExternalId for?

back.answer: An agreed secret string used with third parties to block the confused deputy problem.
back.explanation: The target account can also require MFA in the trust policy.

cards.front: What does IAM Identity Center provide?

back.answer: Single sign-on: one login, a portal, access to multiple AWS accounts and business apps.
back.explanation: Under the hood it assumes roles in each account for you.

cards.sourceHeading: IAM Identity Center (the artist formerly known as AWS SSO)

cards.front: How does IAM Identity Center federate with Okta, Azure AD or on-prem AD?

back.answer: Via SAML 2.0; employees keep corporate passwords and disabling them in the IdP closes all AWS access.
back.explanation: SAML is the XML handshake where one system vouches for a user. AWS never stores the password.

cards.sourceHeading: IAM Identity Center (the artist formerly known as AWS SSO)

cards.front: IAM Identity Center vs Cognito: which federates whom?

back.answer: Identity Center = workforce SSO to AWS accounts; Cognito = app customers (Google/Facebook sign-in).

cards.sourceHeading: IAM Identity Center (the artist formerly known as AWS SSO)

cards.front: How do you require MFA for a sensitive action in an IAM policy?

back.answer: Use condition key aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent set to true.
back.explanation: E.g. deny s3:DeleteObject unless it is true.

cards.front: IAM root account: can policies restrict it, and what are the best practices?

back.answer: Only an SCP can cap it (never in the management account). Enable MFA, delete access keys, don't use daily, root-only tasks only.
back.explanation: Create an admin IAM identity for daily work. Root tasks: closing the account, changing support plans.

cards.front: IAM Access Analyzer vs credentials report / access advisor?

back.answer: Access Analyzer finds resources shared externally; credentials report/access advisor show stale users and unused permissions.
back.explanation: The latter are the least-privilege cleanup answers.

cards.front: An application on EC2 needs to write to DynamoDB. Most secure way to provide credentials?

back.answer: IAM role attached to the instance (instance profile).
back.explanation: Never access keys on the box.

choices.why: Keys on the box can leak.

choices.text: Access keys baked into the AMI
Root account keys in a config file

cards.front: A Lambda function must read from an S3 bucket. How should it authenticate?

back.answer: Lambda execution role with S3 read permissions.

choices.text: IAM user password in env vars

choices.why: Function assumes the role each run.

cards.front: Users in Account A need temporary access to resources in Account B.

back.answer: Role in Account B trusting Account A; users AssumeRole via STS.

choices.why: Role must live in the target account.

choices.text: Role in B with trust for A; AssumeRole
Copy IAM users into Account B

cards.front: A user's identity policy allows s3:PutObject but uploads fail with Access Denied.

back.answer: Look for an explicit Deny — bucket policy, SCP, or permission boundary.
back.explanation: Explicit Deny always beats Allow.

choices.text: Add another Allow to the user
Look for explicit Deny, SCP or boundary

cards.front: An action works in a standalone account but fails in an account inside AWS Organizations.

back.answer: A Service Control Policy is blocking it.
back.explanation: "Organizations" is the tell.

cards.front: Developers create IAM roles for apps, but those roles must never exceed a defined permission set.

back.answer: Permission boundaries.
back.explanation: "Maximum permissions" / "cannot exceed" is the signal.

cards.front: 5,000 employees with Active Directory logins need access to multiple AWS accounts without IAM users.

back.answer: IAM Identity Center with SAML federation to AD.
back.explanation: Existing directory + multiple accounts + no IAM users.

choices.text: IAM Identity Center with SAML to AD

cards.front: An application needs short-lived credentials that expire automatically.

back.answer: STS AssumeRole.
back.explanation: Temporary/short-lived credentials is STS's product.

cards.front: Users may terminate EC2 instances only if signed in with MFA. How?

back.answer: Policy Condition with aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent.
back.explanation: Sensitive action + MFA = that condition key.

choices.why: A ceiling, not an MFA check.

cards.front: A new AWS account was just created. What should be done FIRST to secure it?

back.answer: Enable MFA on root, delete/avoid root access keys, create an admin user for daily work.

choices.text: Enable MFA on root; make an admin user

cards.front: Keyword: **"EC2/app needs AWS access, 'most secure'"**

back.answer: Instance role (instance profile), never keys

cards.front: Keyword: **"Lambda needs permissions"**

back.answer: Execution role

cards.front: Keyword: **"Hardcoded / stored access keys"**

back.answer: Wrong — replace with a role

cards.front: Keyword: **"Temporary / short-lived credentials"**

back.answer: STS AssumeRole

cards.front: Keyword: **"Access across AWS accounts"**

back.answer: Role in target account + trust policy

cards.front: Keyword: **"Third party assumes your role safely"**

back.answer: ExternalId in trust policy

cards.front: Keyword: **"Role exists but 'can't be assumed'"**

back.answer: Fix the trust policy

cards.front: Keyword: **"Allow exists but action denied"**

back.answer: Explicit Deny / SCP / permission boundary

cards.front: Keyword: **"Org-wide restriction, applies even to root"**

back.answer: SCP (AWS Organizations)

cards.front: Keyword: **"Cap max permissions of ONE user/role"**

back.answer: Permission boundary

cards.front: Keyword: **"Policy on the resource, has a Principal"**

back.answer: Resource-based policy (e.g., bucket policy)

cards.front: Keyword: **"Legacy S3 grant mechanism, avoid"**

back.answer: S3 ACL (≠ Network ACL)

cards.front: Keyword: **"SSO, one login → many AWS accounts"**

back.answer: IAM Identity Center

cards.front: Keyword: **"Federate Okta / Azure AD / corporate AD"**

back.answer: IAM Identity Center + SAML 2.0

cards.front: Keyword: **"Federate app customers (Google/Facebook login)"**

back.answer: Cognito

cards.front: Keyword: **"Require MFA for an action"**

back.answer: Condition: aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent

cards.front: Keyword: **"Root account"**

back.answer: MFA on, no access keys, don't use daily

cards.front: Keyword: **"Who is my resource shared with externally?"**

back.answer: IAM Access Analyzer

cards.front: Keyword: **"Find unused users / stale permissions"**

back.answer: Credentials report / access advisor
